stories.title: Bangladesh's external debt increases almost threefold in decade

stories.title: Iqbal and the Pakistani dream: fact or fiction?
summary: For starters, separate statehood was not floated by Iqbal first: right-wing activist Murtaza Ahmad Khan Maikash wrote it up in a four-part-series in Lahore’s daily Inqilab in 1928, premised on the same four provinces that make up Pakistan today.

While Rahmat Ali and the angry young men of Cambridge were calling for a Pakistan that stood severed, the Round Tablers—Iqbal, Jinnah, and Zafrulla Khan—wanted Muslim security inside a federal India, secured by strong provinces and a weak centre.
That’s why, at least up to 1934, Iqbal kept a safe distance from ‘the scheme of Pakistan’.

stories.title: Bumpy road to export-led growth
summary: According to the World Bank’s 1993 study, The East Asian Miracle, countries such as South Korea and Taiwan combined export expansion with industrial investment, technological upgrading and productivity growth.

Unlike East Asian economies, which linked industrial support to productivity and export performance, Pakistan has continued to protect established industries without consistently requiring technological advancement or international competitiveness.

Unless industrial policy and investment incentives are linked to measurable improvements in productivity, domestic value addition, technological upgrading and export performance, ambitious targets may continue to outpace the economy’s capacity to deliver.

summary: A cynical explanation is that the country’s problems — poverty, hunger, lack of education, and health facilities, malnutrition, growing population numbers — don’t affect the power elite, so if they fester there is no skin off its back.

stories.title: Climate change leads to early cotton sowing in Sindh
summary: LAHORE: In a significant shift driven by changing climatic patterns, cotton sowing has begun for the first time during the second week of November in several coastal areas of Sindh, marking a major departure from traditional agricultural practices.

Traditionally, Pakistan had two distinct cotton-growing zones: the coastal districts of Sindh, where sowing began in February and March, and the rest of the country, where planting took place from May 1 to the first week of June.

However, reports indicate that favourable temperatures during the second week of November have encouraged farmers in the coastal districts of Thatta and Sujawal, including Chuhar Jamali, Mirpur Sakro, Gharo, Buhara, Keti Bunder and Chhachh Jahan, to begin cotton sowing.
